In [[algebra]], the '''fixed-point subring''' <math>R^f</math> of an [[automorphism]] ''f'' of a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] ''R'' is the [[subring]] of the [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]]s of ''f'', that is,
:<math>R^f = \{ r \in R \mid f(r) = r \}.</math>
More generally, if ''G'' is a [[group (mathematics)|group]] [[group action|acting]] on ''R'', then the subring of ''R''
:<math>R^G = \{ r \in R \mid g \cdot r = r \ \text{ for all } \ g \in G \}</math>
is called the '''fixed subring''' or, more traditionally, the '''ring of invariants''' under {{mvar|G}}. If ''S'' is a set of automorphisms of ''R'', the elements of ''R'' that are fixed by the elements of ''S'' form the ring of invariants under the group generated by ''S''. In particular, the fixed-point subring of an automorphism ''f'' is the ring of invariants of the [[cyclic group]] generated by ''f''.

In [[Galois theory]], when ''R'' is a [[field (mathematics)|field]] and ''G'' is a group of field automorphisms, the fixed ring is a [[field extension|subfield]] called the '''fixed field''' of the automorphism group; see [[Fundamental theorem of Galois theory]].

Along with a [[module of covariants]], the '''ring of invariants''' is a central object of study in [[invariant theory]]. Geometrically, the rings of invariants are the coordinate rings of (affine or projective) [[GIT quotient]]s and they play fundamental roles in the constructions in [[geometric invariant theory]].

'''Example''': Let <math>R = k[x_1, \dots, x_n]</math> be a [[polynomial ring]] in ''n'' variables. The [[symmetric group]] S<sub>''n''</sub> acts on ''R'' by permuting the variables. Then the ring of invariants <math>R^G = k[x_1, \dots, x_n]^{\operatorname{S}_n}</math> is the [[ring of symmetric polynomials]]. If a [[reductive algebraic group]] ''G'' acts on ''R'', then the [[First and second fundamental theorems of invariant theory|fundamental theorem of invariant theory]] describes the generators of ''R''<sup>''G''</sup>.

[[Hilbert's fourteenth problem]] asks whether the ring of invariants is finitely generated or not (the answer is affirmative if ''G'' is a reductive algebraic group by Nagata's theorem.) The finite generation is easily seen for a [[finite group]] ''G'' acting on a [[finitely generated algebra]] ''R'': since ''R'' is [[integral element|integral]] over ''R''<sup>''G''</sup>,<ref>Given ''r'' in ''R'', the polynomial <math>\prod_{g \in G} (t - g \cdot r)</math> is a monic polynomial over ''R''<sup>''G''</sup> and has ''r'' as one of its roots.</ref> the [[Artin–Tate lemma]] implies ''R''<sup>''G''</sup> is a finitely generated algebra. The answer is negative for some [[unipotent group]]s.

Let ''G'' be a finite group. Let ''S'' be the symmetric algebra of a finite-dimensional [[G-module|''G''-module]]. Then ''G'' is a reflection group if and only if <math>S</math> is a [[free module]] (of finite [[Free_module#Definition|rank]]) over ''S''<sup>''G''</sup> (Chevalley's theorem).{{citation needed|date=September 2015}}<!--Let ''G'' be a finite group and ''V'' a finite-dimensional ''G''-module. Then ''G'' acts on the [[ring of polynomial functions]] on ''V'' as a [[left regular representation]]. [[Molien's formula]] says
:-->

In [[differential geometry]], if ''G'' is a [[Lie group]] and <math>\mathfrak{g} = \operatorname{Lie}(G)</math> its [[Lie algebra]], then each principal ''G''-bundle on a [[manifold]] ''M'' determines a [[Graded ring|graded]] [[algebra homomorphism]] (called the [[Chern–Weil homomorphism]])
:<math>\mathbb{C}[\mathfrak{g}]^G \to \operatorname{H}^{2*}(M; \mathbb{C})</math>
where <math>\mathbb{C}[\mathfrak{g}]</math> is the [[ring of polynomial functions]] on <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> and ''G'' acts on <math>\mathbb{C}[\mathfrak{g}]</math> by [[adjoint representation]].
